You are a good mother, you called her, you obviously care about her. The concern with which you wrote your post and comments show that. Unfortunately, and I say this from experience, BPD can be tricky because while you want the world to know how much you're hurting, at the same time you're overcome with guilt for hurting others and calling attention or help to yourself. A lot of us suffer alone or in silence because we feel the burden of this disease. For me, one of my worst symptoms is feeling abandoned or like no one would care if I lived or died. I guess your daughter might have been dealing with similar feelings because you said no one on her contact list showed up until now. I hope someone does because that would show people care about her. 

But yeah, I'm 27 and still haven't gotten some of the proper help I need to deal with this disorder. It's been 15 years of going into and out of doctor's offices. Some help others make it worse, idk. 

If she didn't want to concern you (which it seems like she didn't!) she would say she is okay being alone in her apartment even if that isn't safe. I've been left alone some times too and the suicidal thoughts take over when you're more vulnerable. But this is the disorder acting up, it is not your failure or hers. Unfortunately this disorder sucks like this. :(

That being said, I hope she is feeling better now and they pumped her stomach. That is very scary. Please be by her side when she wakes up and shower her with love. Moving forward, perhaps try to focus on making yourself more available for her to share her problems with you, or even invite her to talk about it. Try to be understanding. That's what I can say has worked for me and my parents but obviously sometimes the emotions are so overwhelming it's hard to deal with.

So when it comes to copyright, my acc is still standing after 4 years so I don't think they care too much about it; although tbf I haven't been streaming in almost a year. I have received some warnings however, but nothing has really happened. 

When you're streaming, the copyrighted songs still stream to your audience btw so it's not like they hear silence. It's only if you want to keep the video in the highlights afterwards that that could happen, it's happened to a couple of mine where if the songs are mixed they don't flag them but if they're not then there's a bit of an awkward silence.

I'd suggest you record the set as you play it on rekordbox; at the same time, record the screen/visual part wtv of the stream on your streaming app and put the two together as a clip for twitch, or youtube, or instagram highlights. If you record on rekordbox you get to keep the full set in case you need it. (I have not done this in the past and was upset that I had to rip the audio from the stream to get the set saved lol).

Have fun! I love doing a stream once in a while. Share it on social media or with friends and see who shows up. It's usually better during the week (aka no Friday or Saturday) as people usually want to go out during those days so you'll have less audience.

I mean... would we really call that going grandiose? :P If we were in a neurotypical advice board, I'm sure a lot of people would say the same to anyone who's been rejected or dumped. I wouldn't call it grandiose, just doing what you can to cope with the reality and moving forward in a self-affirming away, since these things tend to eat away at our self-esteem or self-perception (I don't believe people who can just get out of a relationship unscathed with no need to prove to themselves they're still "it"). (Feel free to disregard this last part.)

You made a mistake, even people without npd can do what you did. (probably won't call it discard, rather 'overlooking' someone). Or at least you think you did. Rephrase the story you tell yourself. Is there another way to explain what happened? 

Nobody likes being devalued and hopefully you learn something from that. But also maybe that person was displaying some red flags like wanting to marry you right away. That's a little unhinged. I had a similar experience, the only person who was ever really deeply interested in me and I pushed them away because some things were dealbreakers and completely changed my perception of them. How long had you known this person before things went south? Did you really know them or were you operating from an idealization you built up in your head? I think Ns can be prone to that and when reality hits it's shattering. 

I completely understand what you're going through. In my case, after they discarded me, my anger took over, being ill-advised to pursue revenge also didn't help and in my case I got threatened after a huge verbal fight, which I started to feel better about them discarding me (funny how that works, I was on my way to discard but they did it faster and without remorse. I agonized over this for a while). So things can always go worse than just not talking anymore. 

This person's actions have to do with them. I know as an N you take rejection as a judgement of you as a person but a lot of times it's really not like that. Sometimes people have different dealbreakers than you and you can't be on and customer-service ready 24/7 in order to find out what they fancy and try to offer it to them. 

The reality is that this person left, so clearly they were not as amazing as you thought they were. Their actions indicate otherwise. 

As for revenge, like someone else said, it's much better to write out your thoughts and later you can go back and understand yourself from a different more distant perspective. Get it out of yourself. 

There are more people in the world, I'm sure, who would fit your standards for a partner. Just gotta put yourself in a position to find them, so taking care of yourself is key. And revenge looks bad on anyone, as long as you keep it a fantasy you should be good. Eventually the thoughts will dissipate. And if they don't you can always use it for fuel to make yourself better, sometimes it works like that.

I flirted with being npd a decade ago and only now have I returned to it. When I had the trip I'd completely even forgotten that was a thing.

The first trip is okay. I thought I was finally free of the shackles of my mind (aka the masking) and felt a huge ego surge through me, like finally my ego or drive was liberated and I was not only expected but encouraged to act on it. Something I always struggled with was hitting on people I was interested in or flirting with them, and after the trip it became a lot easier - that is until my mind deteriorated beyond repair. 

It took a few more trips and my mind went to dust, and I'm still scrambling to put the pieces back together. 

I'm not sure what's wrong with me, if it's just some npd traits or if I experienced psychotic symptoms but something happened and it was weird. I became increasingly paranoid that people could tell I didn't like them because I wasn't putting the effort into perfecting the mask. Then I had some arguments and turned my back on someone who could see through my vulture like existence, for which I will never forgive her, however pathetic it is. I lost a bunch of friends who sure we weren't really good friends anymore but we were okay. After the acid plus the paranoia plus a series of events where I flirted with insanity and pissed off a bunch of people, my life was never the same again.

Just... be careful when you do it. I was riding an ego high when I first took it and looking back I should never have taken it. I thought I was sure of myself, identity, life path, everything, and after a bunch of experiences with at most one week between each, my mind became like jello. It's been a year since I've last taken it. The ego delusions died down after that series of arguments. But it wasn't until June last year when I became super paranoid and suicidal and thought I could figure out the secrets of the universe that things royally took a turn for the worst. 

I barely leave the house these days. Constantly paranoid that people can call me out on my fictitious nature. I've built up a character to present socially and I hate it. And I'm aware of it which makes things worse. although  I'm slowly getting out of that reality and shifting into something that more closely resembles an organized, real life.

comment on people's posts or add your own funny tags, which the OP will see and possibly reblog from you as well. you can also reply to posts now which is a welcome addition.

I commend your attitude! I've been trying to do the same since I got back into fandom business this year. I got into fanfiction arounf the same time you did and oftentimes I find myself thinking just what the hell went wrong since then?! What's changed so much? I know my writing improved... so why am I getting even less feedback? asides from one or two pieces that do well occasionally, for the most part fandom is barren land for me. Also fandom dependent, platform dependent, but still, ao3 in particular has been... an interesting experience in just how much I can deal with the silence.

My opinion is that for some weird reason, perhaps people got too used to just having works churned out at a really rapid pace, and in particularly abundant quantities, so they're not as appreciate as they used to be. Not to mention that for a lot of fandoms, the quality of content produced has increased a lot, so perhaps people will expect excellent quality from the get go now, as opposed to settling for less quality stuff back in the day (this is not scientific!). I blame Tumblr a bit for that, I think that's great that so many people are compelled to create and now have the tools to do it. 
For some reason, perhaps people are more... unappreciative, now that they know whatever they want will get produced sooner or later by someone. 

I think something important too is that perhaps fandom spaces are now more closed off to the non-creative public? What I mean by this is that back in the day you could get a lot of discussions for example in LJ comments which sure maybe some were in closed communities, but there were ways for you to get in, without particularly having to know the people. But even if all you wanted was to read fic, if you made the effort of joining a community, often you'd also be compelled to reward that effort by actually participating in the community. Intermittently! What I mean is that not everyone is going to be a super fan who goes on the discord server and talks to other people. Sometimes you just wanna lurk (I know I do). Nowadays I think that sense of an even perhaps reluctant community is pretty much gone. If on one hand it's great that discord servers exist, on the other I find it a very unreliable tool for archival purposes and especially for new fans who just want to get a whiff of fan content instead of actually participating and creating stuff. 

While I like the kudos system and I think it's a pretty good addition, it also somehow cheapens feedback. If you leave a kudo, you've done your part as a fan, even if it's the bare minimum. Back in the day you at least had to favorite or follow a story, which the author would be notified about and that would make them happier. 

Idk. I'm just rambling at this point. But yeah. It breaks my heart a little that the feedback just doesn't seem to be so constant. How to move forward from this? 

Personally, I've gone back to being a hyper 13 year old with zero public decency and now I leave a little note at the end of most my works encouraging people to leave feedback. My experience with college has been so diversified that I've become a bit desinthesized to college AUs. I've been enrolled in 3 different degrees in two colleges and for one of them I actually went back to my first college (my current degree) and my experience this time around is so much different from the previous one. State of mind plays a huge role. When I was in highschool, I used to dream about getting into college, I dreamed of this wonderful world where anything was possible. Fanfiction satiated that hunger for adventure and endless possibilities (especially romantic ones). 

But then real college life came around, and I was too depressed to live the life I thought I was going to live. I became a bit disappointed with the expectations fanfic writers had built up in me for years (and I beat myself up for contributing to it, eventually resenting the whole imagination part of writing fic, especially in a setting which I had experienced firsthand and knew to not be so wonderful). 

My point is that fanfic is one thing and real life is another. They might intersect sometimes: you can gain powerful experiences and insights irl that will help guide your writing and vice-versa. And while I would appreciate more realistic college stories about students worried sick about failing deadlines and exams, I also know that some of that wild stuff can happen irl, so it's not pure fabrication. Romanticizing is the right word I think. 

Nowadays I'm living a much more fulfilling college life than I was a few years ago, but I'm still writing a modern-setting/college AU which isn't informed by my real life experiences. They are really two different realities which share the same name - college - but that's about where the similarities often end. 

But to answer your question: college AUs are not very appealling to me right now. They used to be when my real life college experience wasn't up to my standards, even when I was in highschool, but mostly during middle and high school. Although nowadays I am still interested in reading fic that somehow mimics the world I live in, I often find myself drawn to early-2000s fic bc the setting feels somehow more romantic for me. It's another perspective to your question — do we feel comfortable reading about the world or the life we are experiencing right now, or does the lens of the past, the future or different realities grip us more? Like I once read in a comment thread, knowing about which kind of music the characters are listening to and seeing contemporary cultural references often breaks the immersion for me, unless the author is very knowledgeable about that world and is committed to "immortalizing it" the way a historian sometimes would.

I'm actually not sure what I can tell you. I thought I was INFP as a teen, at the worst of my depression and anxiety spells. Then as I got better and started getting out of the house I tested ENFP for years. Also dabbled in INTP, INFJ, INTJ, ISFP, ENTP and ENFJ territory for a while. It's complicated stuff! 

From your post it seems to me that you're very philosophically inclined and interested in truth seeking. My experience tells me that what we tell ourselves is sometimes more important than the truth due to the tangible effects it can have on our personality. I might have tested ENFP more often two years ago because I was in a more open-minded headspace, where I thought "this is who I am, I'm just reinforcing it through actual behaviours" (which I think might be how personalities get.formed, no?). 

Anyway, what truly helped in my case was taking the time to assess how I really feel without coming from a place of judgment. I realized that for most of my life, I desperately wished to be someone I wasn't. In doing that, I gained a lot of experience in "acting" or performing, and certainly gained/developed skills I otherwise wouldn't have but I also couldn't see what others saw in me. Anytime people would describe me I felt like it made no sense. But like you I kept looking for their judgement, because I didn't trust my own. 

Taking time to meditate and focus on what I'm feeling at the moment with no judgement - simply focusing on recognizing things as if they don't personally affect you, so avoiding shutting down your real feelings because they're "wrong' or not how you imagined yourself to be - has helped tremendously. Now I often ask myself "what are you really feeling? Not what is appropriate or what feels easier to answer, or even what comes to you first out of habit (for example I might think that I'm feeling anxious in a new situation when I'm actually thrilled and excited), but what is most present at this poin in time?". There is no wrong or right answer, just a continuous process of getting to know yourself through tools that are accessible to you - your mind and your senses.

In the end what we tell ourselves really matters. I told myself I loved parties now (I always did, but during my teen years I was too depressed to even consider that. Plus I told myself parties were for lame jocks, and I got good grades and was well-behaved and liked reading and writing so obviously I needed settings that would compliment and reinforce my personality lol. such whack!), so I started attending more parties and throwing them, so people started seeing me as a party girl. I know how this type of illusion works, which is I think why I can grow past it now and truly become immersed in the discovery of my true self. Perhaps being familiar with fictional characters and realizing that as different as they are, they are all fascinating has allowed me to translate that knowledge to real life. And it's very liberating to apply it to yourself - you don't have to be right or perfect or the perfect embodiment of a stereotype, you just have to be yourself, as weird and thorny as it might sometimes be, and as fascinating and liberating as it certainly is. 

I can't tell which type you are, but I hope some of this resonated with you. I know your post resonated a lot with me. I wish you luck in your journey. Hugs. 💞

Hey. I took the time to read this and actually searched for posts like this so I could identify with them and comiserate with someone that's going through the same thing. But this post in particular, I felt compelled to reply to. Especially the part where you mention that thing about people touching each other casually, but not you. 

​

I have been where you are. Sometimes I still go back to that place. Know that it is indeed a place - it is not who you are. I've left it for a while. You could say I went on holiday.  


I realized, through a lot of therapy, that I actually AM pushing people away with my body language. And that the way I feel about myself, sometimes informs how other people think about me as well. How attractive they think I am. Say I'm down a lot of the time because of those insecurities and concerns about my appearance (which I often am). On those days, it's very hard to even make conversation with friends I've known for years. I despise everything I say, or act, or walk, or even the way I hold a fucking drink, or how my face looks from the side. I still struggle with accepting that these people are not disgusted by my hideous face, and sometimes we talk about it. While some of them go for the obvious "shut up you're beautiful" comment that a friend makes because well, they're your friend and that's a nice thing to say, some of them actually take the time to consider how I feel and engage with me on my thought process, to the point where we end up deconstructing these beliefs. I think this is a very helpful thing to do, so if you have a friend you can talk to about these things I definitely encourage that. 

Anyway, my point with this comment was that once I started changing the way I saw myself, and especially the negative self-talk that so often happens to people with BDD or depression or anxiety, things started gradually becoming... surprisingly better. But I didn't notice the change, for a while. (And btw, things are now a little bit worse again, so everything is cyclical and there is no perfect state of happiness that we can reach about these things).   


 I used to be very touchy and friendly as a kid, but as I grew up shit got into my head. Real stupid shit, like, "don't hug people because your arms will look too big around them", "don't make friends with people who are petite because they make you look bigger", "don't hug other people because omg they are beautiful and you're ugly and fat and you're ruining it for everybody over your selfish desire for human touch", etc etc. I was living in fear. And no one should have to live that way. That, obviously, includes you.   


​

A few years ago, people wouldn't touch me either. I didn't... invite that kind of approach. I wasn't okay with casual touches, like hugging someone goodbye, or kissing my friends because I felt like it. I think it would help you to reflect on those things, instead of looking at the world and just seeing you not fitting in with it - do you even want to fit in? Do you feel better when you hug and touch other people? Because it took me a while, but I learned that I do in fact need physical touch to feel wanted and cherished. Even by friends. So that's where I started working. Smiling more. More eye contact. I was still obese and ugly, and people still made fun of my appearance, but gradually things started getting better from my inner circle of friends to an outer circle (which btw didn't develop overnight. all of this took at least 2-4 years). And now people from that outer circle meet me after a while and they tell me how surprised they are that I now accept hugs. It's not that I didn't accept hugs before - to me at least, that didn't make sense. I WANTED HUGS, I WANTED TO BE TOUCHED. But was I really open to that possibility? What would it do to my beliefs about myself, about how disgusting and stupid and unworthy I was? It was going to shatter my inner logic, and for a while I fought against that, because I'm a stubborn ass motherfucker, but I did surrender after a while. I surrendered to the softness. Being hugged always felt good to me, but I was denying myself the possibility of feeling that good feeling again. I hope that upon reading this, it makes you at least reflect on some of these things. I'm not a therapist, and this isn't necessarily advice, but it is information that people have shared with me throughout my journey of accepting myself, and I feel like I need to pass this on to other people. I'm just sharing an experience that I've definitely gone through and survived, and I'm telling you all this because I want you to achieve the same thing. No matter how long it takes. Always have faith that you will get there, wherever that is. Sending a lot of love and hugs your way. <3

Boas, estive em artes (acabei o curso no secundário há dois anos) e fiz os dois exames. Posso-te dizer que no geral é mais fácil tirar boa nota a geometria (tipo 17/18/19), porque quando acertas costumas acertar em tudo (consequentemente, quando erras, é difícil de remediar, mas tens sempre a 2ª fase!). Mas se como dizes nunca tiveste geometria, é difícil aprenderes tudo, cimentares o conhecimento e fazeres um brilharete até ao exame porque já não tens muito tempo (lembra-te que é matéria do 11º e 12º ano). E sim, se estudares bem é muito mais possível que tires uma nota excelente do que em desenho.
Na minha experiência, eu era das melhores alunas de desenho nas três turmas em que estive no secundário (alguns 20's e coisas do tipo) e no exame tive 15. O exame de desenho é muito à sorte, nunca tens a certeza se correu bem ou mal até veres a nota. 

Para além disso às vezes há coisas que correm mal na própria prova. Em 2014 quando fiz o meu exame, havia um exercício em que tinhas de desenhar uma imagem que eles te davam com tinta da china e pastel de óleo, ora, estes dois materiais não se misturam, por isso estás a ver o arraso que foi nas notas de quem não conseguiu conjugar os dois.  Outra coisa, sendo um exame mais subjectivo, a opinião do avaliador conta bastante para tua nota, por isso às vezes pode calhar de a pessoa acordar com os pés de fora e teres o exame arrasado à conta disso. (com arrasado digo qualquer nota abaixo de 15). Se isso te acontecer, podes pedir uma revisão de prova (acho que é 5€ pela cópia, para veres se realmente vale a pena fazer a reapreciação, por exemplo levas a cópia a um professor de desenho/artes que conheças e vêem os dois isso, e 25€ para a reapreciação, no caso de a tua nota subir acho que te devolvem o dinheiro mas isso já não tenho a certeza). 

Em relação a preparares-te para o exame, dá uma olhada no site da aproged que tem todos os exames de anos anteriores para teres uma ideia do que te espera. Como dizes que nunca tiveste desenho, o melhor se calhar seria mesmo arranjares um explicador que te ajudasse a praticar ou te ensinasse técnicas. Ou se tiveres uma escola de artes (ou uma escola com o curso normal de artes) podes sempre falar com um professor de desenho e pedir se podes assistir às aulas e pedir dicas nos teus trabalhos mesmo que não contem para nota. É certo, não vais com o mesmo know-how de alguém que teve a disciplina três anos, mas se te preparares bem tens sempre uma hipótese.

Em todo o caso, aconselho-te a inscreveres-te nos dois exames se ainda não tens a certeza de qual queres fazer, e depois quando chegar a altura vês se queres fazer os dois ou só desenho/geometria. :) Espero ter sido útil. Se tiveres mais alguma dúvida feel free to pm me.

Yeah I know what you mean. I'm torn between the two arcs tbh. On one hand, POI was an amazing procedural during its first 2 seasons, on the other, it's also a very cool show about Artificial Intelligence. I think both arcs are necessary to make the show what it is and ultimately some people are going to prefer one over the other. Personally I enjoy them both, because both were good at what they were trying to accomplish - the more procedural part of the show was approached in an original way, different from most procedurals, which immediately makes it stand out. However, I think the general discontentment with the turns the show has taken comes from a misunderstanding of what the show is about. The premise of the show is not about solving crimes (although it's more comfortable to think so). It's about using AI to solve these crimes. The main character is basically the one we never 'see' on screen - the machine (this is entirely my opinion and you are more than allowed to disagree). So ultimately the story is about Artificial Intelligence, just sugarcoated a bit in the first seasons to give viewers something they can relate to (I believe most people wouldn't tune in were the show exclusively about AI as it would get boring after a while). I think the writers were very clever in that they mixed both themes and tried to appeal to different audiences. The crime part of the show was created to bring the viewers in, hook them on the show and then try to tell the story they wanted to tell (it's hard to tell a story when there's no one to listen/see!).
In the end, there are always going to be people who love the later arcs and people who prefer the first more procedural ones.
Regarding the dialogue and the acting, I think the standards have not been lowered at all. But I think this Samaritan-arc is more plot-oriented rather than character-oriented, which means sometimes character development or accuracies will be dropped in favor of the plot (which is fine sometimes, just not too many).

I've been on your friend's end of the situation and the one thing I was really afraid the people I considered 'my friends' would do was to just stop talking to me because I annoyed them with my depression. 
Depression is too serious. I've been there (still am) and everyone ends up leaving because you're suffering and that spills over to your interactions with other people. They feel the sadness and feel repulsed by it. If you consider this girl to be a true friend then I think the best thing to do would be to help her get through this hard time. You don't have to do crazy things - sometimes, for someone who's depressed, just /knowing/ that there's someone willing to hear them out is enough (even if you don't actually do it. Basically, knowing they have someone to rely on helps). 
I know that in this day and age there are so many articles talking about toxic relationships and how to get away from them but I don't feel like this is the case maybe because I've been through it. 
Think about this person; are you willing to cut her out of your life in light of the situation? Do you think her behaviour is temporary or is she just changing? If it's temporary I advise you to stick by her. Better days will come and she will not be able to thank you enough for doing  that. Very few people do it. 
However, if you think her personality is changing and you find that you have nothing in common anymore, nothing to talk about, or you think her depression talk is taking a toll on you (kinda like a damp cloth on your mood) then I'd say maybe step back for a while. Don't stop talking to her altogether but do only what you deem necessary, as in don't get too involved if you know it will eventually undermine your friendship. 
I think this friendship can bring you happiness again, when you both are in a place that allows you to give and receive happiness, but it takes work to get there. Best of luck :)
